preamble: To mark the centenary of Philip Larkin's birth

clue.text: Very bad criminal hid silver with no end of liquor

indicators.note: criminal hints that the letters have been bent out of their honest order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: with no says the following letter is missing from silver

parts.note: taken as written, before its last letter goes

indicators.note: end of picks the final letter of the word liquor

parts.note: its final letter is the one removed

explanation.surface: A villain who stashed the silver and drank the liquor dry is up to no good.
explanation.walkthrough: SILVER loses its R (the end of liquor) to leave SILVE; that and HID are rearranged, as 'criminal' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish describes something wicked or fiendish, so it serves as a synonym for very bad.

clue.text: Sound of indifference about small network

indicators.note: about places the indifferent sound around the letter for small

parts.note: meh is the shrugging sound of someone who does not care
S is the standard clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a modest social or computer network.
explanation.definitionFit: A mesh is a net-like interlaced structure, a network of connected strands or nodes.

clue.text: Graduate in French department has work for early morning

indicators.note: in places the graduate's letters inside the name of the department

parts.note: the Aude is a department in southern France
a BA, a Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: A graduate working in a French department turns out a piece at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Larkin's poem 'Aubade' is one of the themed answers; Aude is an administrative department of France.
explanation.definitionFit: An aubade is a poem or song greeting the dawn, a piece composed for daybreak.

clue.text: Manage to probe corrupt deal somewhere in West Sussex

indicators.note: to probe means to go inside, so this word enters the rearranged letters
corrupt suggests the letters of deal have been tampered with

parts.note: taken as written
to run a business is to manage it

explanation.surface: A manager investigates a crooked deal somewhere in the south of England.
explanation.walkthrough: DEAL is rearranged to ADEL ('corrupt'), and RUN goes into it. West Sussex is a county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Arundel is a town in West Sussex, known for its castle, so it is an example of a place there.

clue.text: Controversy in Scottish city after dumping fish

indicators.note: after dumping says the city's name is left once the fish is thrown away

parts.note: Stirling is a city in central Scotland
a ling is a long, cod-like sea fish

explanation.surface: A row breaks out in a Scottish city after fish is dumped.
explanation.definitionFit: A stir is a commotion or public fuss, the excitement a controversy causes.

clue.text: Embarrassed North American sadly overturned portable stove

indicators.note: overturned in a down clue means the whole string is read from the bottom up

parts.note: embarrassed people go red
N is the compass abbreviation for North
alas is said sadly, an expression of grief

explanation.surface: A red-faced American regrets knocking over a camping stove.
explanation.walkthrough: RED + N + AM + ALAS is written upwards; 'sadly' looks like an anagram signal but supplies ALAS.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides the lizard-like amphibian, a salamander is a portable heater or stove used for cooking or drying.

clue.text: Tragic female's drug dealing admission?

parts.note: a dealer's confession would be 'I sold'
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A woman confesses to dealing drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the clue as the confession 'I sold E'.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolde is the doomed heroine of the Tristan legend and Wagner's opera, a female tragic figure.

clue.text: Frenchman and German carrying uniform for unprincipled figure?

parts.note: René is a typical French man's name

indicators.note: carrying means the abbreviation for German holds the uniform letter

parts.note: U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Frenchman and a German share a uniform, perhaps as turncoats.
explanation.definitionFit: A reneguer is one who reneges, breaking promises, hence a person lacking principle.

clue.text: Limit leading posters for despicable sorts

indicators.note: leading says the word for limit comes in front of the word for posters

parts.note: to marks a limit, as in 'up to ten'
posters are ads, advertisements

explanation.surface: Someone who restricts bill-posting is a contemptible type.
explanation.walkthrough: Larkin's poem 'Toads' is among the themed answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Toad is a term of abuse for a loathsome person, so toads are contemptible people.

clue.text: Very positive man serving from the East in hotels

indicators.note: in places the soldier inside the pair of hotel letters

parts.note: H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet, so two hotels give HH

indicators.note: from the East means read right to left in an across clue

parts.note: a GI is an American serviceman

explanation.surface: An enlisted man working in hotels is very upbeat.
explanation.walkthrough: IG (GI reversed) goes into HH. With 18 across, Larkin's 'High Windows'.
explanation.definitionFit: High describes elated or excited spirits, an extremely upbeat mood.

clue.text: Only alarm replaced around 5th of October in unusual fashion

indicators.note: around says the rearranged letters wrap the single October letter
replaced means the letters are put back in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: 5th of picks the fifth letter of October

parts.note: its fifth letter is used

explanation.surface: An alarm clock reset around early October behaves oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Replaced' looks like part of the alarm story but signals a rearrangement; 'Only' is part of the fodder, not a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Abnormally means in a way that departs from what is normal, so oddly or strangely.

clue.text: I'm bowled over by craze which deceives viewers

indicators.note: bowled over means turned upside down, so the letters of I'm run backwards

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
a rage is a fashion or craze, as in 'all the rage'

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to being overwhelmed by the latest fad.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, fooling the eye with a false image.

clue.text: One who's learned independently about tuition regularly played a dramatic role

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word tuition

parts.note: its alternate letters are used
someone who played a dramatic role did act

explanation.surface: A self-taught person is said to have acted a part.
explanation.walkthrough: The even letters of tuition give UTO, between A and DID ACT.
explanation.definitionFit: An autodidact is a self-taught person, educated without teachers or formal schooling.

clue.text: European recalled study about Czech, say, enduring oppression?

indicators.note: about means the reversed study surrounds the Czech
recalled means called back, so the letters of the study run backwards

parts.note: a den is a private room for study
a Czech is an example of a Slav

explanation.surface: A European remembers a study about Czechs living under tyranny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Czech, say' signals an example: Czechs are one of the Slav peoples. The reversed study wraps it, leaving its first letter outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Enslaved people are held in bondage, which is a form of severe subjugation.

clue.text: Scottish short story writer missing area gets to go downhill?

indicators.note: missing says the writer's pen name lacks the letter for area

parts.note: Saki was the pen name of H. H. Munro, a short-story writer of Scottish descent

explanation.surface: A Scottish writer lacking space finally gets to slide down a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: To ski is to glide over snow on runners, typically descending a slope.

clue.text: Ingenuity shown by relative, it's said, in festival

indicators.note: it's said means the two words are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: wit is ingenuity and a son is a relative, giving WIT SON

explanation.surface: A clever relative is admired at a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: WIT SON spoken aloud matches the festival. With 21 across, Larkin's 'The Whitsun Weddings'.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitsun, or Pentecost, is a Christian feast seven weeks after Easter.

clue.text: Vase concealed by furniture

indicators.note: concealed by says the answer lies hidden inside the next word

parts.note: the letters lie within this word

explanation.surface: A vase is tucked away behind the furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: An urn is a vase-like container, often with a foot, used for ashes or decoration.

clue.text: Those with mates passed around note giving periods of opportunity

indicators.note: around says the bereaved people surround the letter for note

parts.note: widows are women whose spouses have died

explanation.surface: Bereaved partners pass round a note offering chances.
explanation.definitionFit: A window is a limited span of time when something is possible, as in a launch window.

clue.text: Dramatist, one inventing a plot, reported for youthful indiscretions?

indicators.note: reported means the names are heard, not spelt

parts.note: Oscar Wilde was a playwright and Titus Oates fabricated the Popish Plot of 1678, giving WILDE OATES

explanation.surface: A playwright and a conspirator are said to have been reckless in youth.
explanation.walkthrough: WILDE OATES spoken aloud sounds like the phrase; Titus Oates invented a Catholic plot against Charles II.
explanation.definitionFit: Sowing one's wild oats is the idiom for indulging in reckless youthful behaviour.

clue.text: Australian unusually cites creed's opening, being of austere outlook

indicators.note: unusually means the letters of cites appear in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: opening picks the first letter of the word creed's

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: An Australian oddly quotes the start of a creed, showing a strict outlook.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascetic means practising strict self-denial, the severe, self-disciplined way of life.

clue.text: Western news chief given new cracking accommodation for events before receptions?

parts.note: ed is the abbreviation for editor, the head of a newspaper

indicators.note: cracking means breaking into, so the new letter goes inside the lodgings

parts.note: digs is British slang for lodgings

explanation.surface: A Western editor is given new, excellent lodgings for functions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' looks like an adjective for the accommodation but signals N going into DIGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Marriage ceremonies normally come before the party, or wedding reception, that follows them.

clue.text: Mature circle disowning Republican

indicators.note: disowning says the letter for Republican is cast off

parts.note: to circle is to revolve

explanation.surface: An established group of friends rejects a Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: To evolve is to develop gradually, as a thing ripens or grows to maturity.

clue.text: Backing for American bank without doubt

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters for American are reversed

parts.note: US stands for American, as in US forces
to bank on something is to rely on it

explanation.surface: Support for an American bank is certain.
explanation.definitionFit: Surely is an adverb for certainty, as in 'surely you know'.

clue.text: Almost realise romantic acquaintance is unexciting

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: to see something is to realise it
a date is someone one is courting

explanation.surface: Someone nearly realises their romantic partner is dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedate means calm and unhurried, so quiet and lacking excitement.

clue.text: Revered figure penning line with series of postings? That's valuable material

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the divine figure holds the line

parts.note: a god is a figure of worship
an online thread is a chain of posts

explanation.surface: An idolised figure writes a line in a forum, producing worthwhile content.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold thread is fine metallic yarn used in luxury embroidery and fabrics, so costly stuff.

clue.text: Transport by road to drop a large ship's frame in port

indicators.note: to drop means the letter a is left out

parts.note: to haul goods is to carry them by lorry
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A road haulier drops off a big ship's frame at the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on both senses: a ship's hull, and Hull, the English port city where Larkin worked as librarian.
explanation.definitionFit: A hull is the main body or shell of a ship, and Hull is also a port on the Humber.

clue.text: One seeking revolution rejected wrong in courts

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the legal term is read backwards

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: A would-be revolutionary has a legal claim thrown out.
explanation.definitionFit: Trot is informal for a Trotskyist, a left-winger who wants overthrow of the system.

clue.text: Place to put stiff and heavy book, not English book

indicators.note: not says the English letter is swapped out for the book letter

parts.note: a tome is a large, weighty volume

explanation.surface: A dull, weighty book puts a reader into a stupor.
explanation.walkthrough: A stiff is slang for a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomb is a vault or grave where a dead body is laid to rest.

clue.text: First of visitors obscuring entrance in pub is outspoken

indicators.note: obscuring the entrance means covering up the first letter of the pub word

parts.note: the local is a British name for one's nearby pub

indicators.note: first of picks the opening letter of visitors

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: The first visitors blocking a pub doorway speak their minds.
explanation.walkthrough: V replaces the L at the start of LOCAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Vocal means expressing opinions openly and loudly, being forthright.

clue.text: Hint for one's confidant

explanation.walkthrough: The verb and noun are pronounced differently.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to imply; as a noun it names a very close personal friend.
